editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.p:
The following oral history testimony is the result of a
audiotaped interview with Robert C. Lawrence conducted by
Tom Swope on April 26, 2002, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral
History Project. The interview took place in Richmond
Heights, Ohio and is part of the Library of Congress
collection of oral testimonies.

The interview was transcribed and processed by
Sherry R. Moody.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is
reading a verbatim transcript of spoken rather than written
prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to
represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a
personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or
edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of place, names,
foreign words, and personal names have been verified either
by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some
uncertainties will inevitable remain regarding some words
and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a
word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
BY MR. SWOPE:
This is the oral history of World War II veteran,
Robert C. Lawrence. Bob served in the U.S. Army,
84th Infantry Division, 333rd Regiment, Company B. He
served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was
sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at
Mr. Lawrence's home in Richmond Heights, Ohio, on
April 26th, 2002. Bob was 76 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Where were you living when the war started?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. I was living in Traverse City, Michigan and Pearl Harbor
occurred, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Do you have specific memories of the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah. I remember that we were flopped on the floor
reading the Sunday comics and I guess had the radio on
and that's when it came over on Sunday afternoon.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. I was born in 1926 so 14. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What did you think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, I remember going to school the next day, and all
the kids were all excited and gung ho, and, of course, we
were too young to do anything about it as far as joining
the service or anything, but we were just excited about
it and interested to find out what was really going on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, I was 18 on March 17th, 1944, and so I immediately
got my draft notice in Traverse City. I was inducted at
Fort Sheridan, Illinois on June 7th, 1944, one day after
D-Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. What was it like going in after -- the day after D-Day
and knowing what was going on over there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, actually I don't remember a heck of a lot about it
right at the moment, what really happened, because we
were so busy traveling down from Traverse City to Fort
Sheridan and getting inducted and then immediately
getting on a troop train and heading off for Camp Blammy
(ph), Florida so it was -- there was just so much going
on that it's not vivid in my memory of D-Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What do you remember about your training?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Oh, I remember that -- this is the summer of '44, and
we're off to Camp Blammy, Florida near Gainesville right
in the center of Florida in the summertime, and we do
infantry basic training. It's like the desert out there
and digging the fox holes and the marches and the training with the rifle on the range and the 25-mile
march at the end and bivouac and so on and just that it
was so hot and humid down there, and, of course, it was
before air conditioner or anything like that, and so we
all lost a considerable amount of weight in doing this
basic training in Florida. So after all this, then
eventually in -- after we got a leave to go home, why,
here we go off to Europe which is where they had the
coldest winter in 20 years so we were all set for the hot
weather.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What was your unit?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. I ended up with Company B of the 333rd Regiment of the
84th Infantry Division. I joined up with them the end of
December 1944. We crossed the Atlantic to South Hampton,
immediately got on a smaller ship and went across the
channel to Le Havre and got on the 40 and 8 boxcars to go
through France and heading down towards Belgium where by
this time the Battle of the Bulge had started while we
were on the ship. So we went in as replacements around
Liege in Belgium where the company had been wiped out on
Christmas Day night, December 25th. They made a marching
attack in some woods down there, and they were actually,
I believe, in Germany then, maybe Belgium. But in any
event they were -- they were massacred. I mean, they
were attacking at night and firing their weapons as they went. Then they were told there were a few German
infantry down there, and when they got there, they ran
into tanks and infantry, and, of course, a lot of them by
then were lost and out of ammunition and so on. So they
lost -- out of their 140 guys in the company, they --
they were down to maybe 40 or something like that. The
rest were wounded and -- wounded and killed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What was your job?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. I was the first platoon of the first squad and just a
rifleman. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So what other memories can you tell me of The Bulge?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, I remember then on -- we were over there the end of
December and sent to the company, and then on New Year's
Eve we were on the front lines down there at midnight,
and at midnight they had the biggest barrage ever, and,
of course, we didn't know if that was coming or going.
So we -- kind of terrifying, but it was a memorable New
Year coming in there, and then January 1st we're -- we're
in the forest in the fox holes, and there was not a lot
of action right then so I have letters still that I wrote
home from when I was sitting in the fox hole writing
letters and send them back up to Michigan, and we were in
the middle of all these tall pine trees so every once in
a while the German 88 artillery would come in in the tree
tops and -- and get -- the shell bursts when it hits the tree tops, and then the shrapnel comes spraying down, and
so several of the fellows were hit by the shrapnel as
they try to get -- get in cover, but it was all coming
right direct from the top so it was hard to avoid a lot
of times, and so we were always digging fox holes and
digging in and moving, and so we just -- just kept going,
and the Battle of the Bulge -- well, I just remember it
was so cold and snowy. As we said, it was the coldest
winter they'd had there in 20 years or something like
that, and we were living outside, and we had these
leather GI shoes, sort of boots but not waterproof by any
means, so most of the guys or a lot of the guys were
getting frozen feet. We had more casualties from that I
think than we did from the enemy action for -- for a
while there. Then eventually they brought us in these
shoe packs which were rubber bottom, leather tops and
felt linings and these were pretty weather proof, but
they came too late for a lot of the guys. But I just
remember we're going through the -- going through the --
the woods and the sergeant saying, "Fix bayonets." That
was one of our first trips through there, and that was
kind of frightening, you know, to figure this is too
close for comfort and -- but nothing materialized from
that. In fact, my bayonet of this M-1 I had picked up
had a defect of a clasp or something, and the bayonet wouldn't even stay on the rifle. So the sergeant was
just saying, "Well, just put it back in the scabbard and
just have it handy in case you need it." Then nothing
much materialized on that one. Then a little later they
said -- of course, there was all kinds of commotion all
over, and they were saying, "You guys got to be ready for
hand-to-hand combat within 24 hours," and we thought we
don't -- we don't particularly care for that idea either.
So in any event within 24 hours we were in the middle of
a small town up there in the midst of the battle, but by
then luckily the Germans were surrendering and coming
down the street with their hands up and -- but it was so
cold and the dead bodies all over the place especially
the German bodies stacked up, you know, just like
cordwood, and we had to ride in two-and-a-half-ton trucks
from place to place, and it was so slippery they were
sliding off the road, and then we rode on -- some on top
of the tanks also, and they were having a hard time, too,
going through the -- through the wintery stuff in the
forest.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. When you got to The Bulge, did it -- did it still seem
pretty bleak as far as what the Germans were doing? Did
it look like the Germans might succeed?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah, it was pretty scary because they were still going
pretty good at the end of December, and they were -- we -- of course, we had to get a new password every night
to stand guard duty and remember the password or the --
they would start shooting, our sentries and so on. They
were telling us about the Germans disguised as Americans,
soldiers, you know, and had to keep an eye out for them.
So it was -- it was pretty scary. It was still going on
pretty strong.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Did you encounter any of those infiltrators firsthand,
your unit?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. I don't -- no, I don't think we did. Huh-uh. No. We
were mainly just -- we went up to Belgium and the
crossroads -- the main crossroads and had to defend those
and -- to keep them opened, main highways, through the
forest there so -- so we could get our counterattacks
going, and then they -- Patton's tanks were part of
our -- we were attached to him for a while and he was
taking off on a rampage, and we were assigned to ride on
a weasel, which is a small-track vehicle, open vehicle,
and they would pile those full of five-gallon Jerry cans
of gasoline, and then they put a couple of us guys with
our M-1s propped up on top of these things as -- as their
armament, you know. So how they -- but he would go till
they ran out of gas and then we would come up with these
weasels with gasoline so he could keep going. But I
remember the -- every once in a while you would have mortars coming in on you, and we'd bail off the top of
those things and head for cover, but -- one of my buddies
was hit by some shrapnel. He was sitting right next to
me, and -- but I was -- luckily nothing -- nothing
happened to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Do you have any other memories, specific memories, of
buddies?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, we had some fox holes buddies that we were with all
the time, and we have since had reunions, and we have a
national reunion every year in different parts of the
country, and then we have a Company B 333rd reunion every
year and more local people -- well, they come from all
over Louisiana, Indiana, and Pennsylvania and so on,
but -- then we move that around too. So I would -- after
I got out, I would search for these buddies and found one
three or four years ago that I hadn't seen in over 50
years so I -- it's always interesting to find them again,
you know, get them active in our reunions.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Before I forget, did you have any close encounters with
Patton? Did you get close to him at all?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. We just -- of course, we never saw him, but we were right
there with his tanks, and we'd just gassed them up and
they would take off, but I remember after we broke
through and even got to the Autobahn, why, what's when we
rode on top of the tanks and went barrelling down the Autobahn heading for -- well, Berlin or bust a little
later on, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So what happened then after The Bulge for you?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Then we were -- of course, we were in Belgium and then we
went into Holland, and we were chasing the Germans out of
the -- around the dikes there, and then we went to the
Rohr (sp) River, and they had -- the Germans had flooded
that area to delay our crossing so we sat around there
for a while and finally were able to cross, and we were
training to go across in the -- in the boats, small
boats, with the guys paddling, but we went through the
next morning when they had foot bridges across there so
we were able to cross pretty easily although there were
still bodies around and so on and -- but then we
proceeded to head for the Rhine River, and we got
pretty -- a pretty -- a pretty fast trip across there
from the Rohr (ph) to the Rhine, and then by then they
had some bridges across the Rhine, and we got across
there okay, and then we had -- we were in the
two-and-a-half-ton trucks with signs on them that said
"Berlin or Bust," and so we proceeded across there and --
pretty fast trip. After we crossed the Rhine, we came to
some small rivers, and they dropped our squad off, our
platoon, to guard these small bridges because the Germans
were still all around, and so they dropped us and they took off and they forgot about us, and so we were there
just guarding those bridges and living off the land and
getting the eggs and the chickens off the local farmer
and so on. Our platoon sergeant was a Sergeant Schume
(ph) who had cousins fighting on the German side over
there at the same time, but he could speak to the farmer
and get us some food, and the farmer was very happy to
give us the food because they had been told we were going
to kill them all. That was pretty good if all we wanted
was a few eggs, you know, or a chicken or something. But
then they reported us as missing in action because we had
been away from the outfit for several days, and
apparently they just forgot where they left us or nobody
kept track of us. So they sent telegrams home "missing
in action" for our platoon. We were scattered around
covering several bridges, and there was a little action
at night. The Germans would try to get across those
bridges. We -- they didn't direct come across ours, but
the other fellows ran into some opposition or did a lot
of shooting at night to keep -- keep them moving, and --
anyway a few days after they sent the telegrams home,
which excited -- got our friends and relatives all
upset -- it was in the local papers and all that -- why,
a couple days later the telegrams came that we were back
with our outfits so -- I still have those telegrams, too, in the stuff that my parents saved, and I have my
scrapbooks. So then we proceeded. We went through a lot
of these German towns and all kinds of commotion there
with the artillery and the tanks and the infantry and the
Creefeld (ph) was one town we went through on the -- in
the late afternoon or night. Everything was a blasting,
and -- and a German infantry soldier came around one of
the buildings and looking right at me, and he wasn't --
he was as surprised to see me as I was to see him so I
just raised my rifle and hollered "Halt" and he turned
around and took off the corner of the building, and
that's the last I saw of him, but -- but then we
proceeded to the Elbe River 50 miles from Berlin
approximately, but we had the agreement to not take
Berlin which was -- made us happy. We didn't care
particularly about going any further. So we just sat on
the Elbe and kept guard at night because the Germans were
coming across in droves trying to escape from the
Russians, you know, and they were crossing the Elbe and
coming to our side. So we took them prisoners and sent
them back to the rear and took their weapons and so we
all got a lot of souvenirs of rifles and pistols and
binoculars and all that stuff off the -- off the Germans
as they were surrendering, and then we -- before long the
Russians appeared on the other side, and our commanding officers, the captains and so on, they would go across in
the boats and greet the Russians, and our platoon
sergeant went across, and they would celebrate and take
pictures and drink a little schnapps and exchange head
wear, their helmets and fur hats and all that, and a lot
of pictures and so on. So we just sat on the Elbe for a
while, and that's where we were when the war ended in
Europe.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. So how much longer did you have to stay over there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, then -- see, this was, what, May when the war
ended, and then they took us down to a little town of
Germany called Luchsosachsen (ph) near Heidelberg and --
as Army of occupation and -- well mainly is retraining
for Japanese tactics. We were doing mostly bayonet
training and stuff like that. And we figured, well, some
of the fellows with a lot of points would go home first
and then come back and go to Japan, but we had so few
points that we just stayed there, and so then the war
ended in, what -- in May I guess, and one of the -- while
there -- yeah, and then it still went on until August, of
course, in Europe. So we were still there training to go
to Japan when the atom bomb is dropped, and then that was
the end of it. Then -- then I stayed the -- another year
in Germany just as Army of occupation which was pretty
good duty because I got to go on leave to the Riviera and Switzerland and the Bavarian Alps and so on so it was
pretty good duty.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. What were the people like to you when you were in the
Army of occupational Germany?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. They were very friendly because we were taking over their
houses, and this -- they had pretty nice houses, all the
modern facilities, but we moved them out in back in the
barns and garages or whatever with the animals, you know,
so they were right by their house, and they had living
facilities back there, but we were right there in their
house, but -- of course, we had orders not to do any
looting or destruction or what have you even if we wanted
to which we didn't so we had no problem with the
Germans -- populace, and especially since our sergeant
spoke German, he became acquainted with a lot of them on
friendly terms, and after the war he made several trips
back there and vice versa. A lot of them came over to
visit him in Van Wert, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. We talked earlier about writing letters. What kind of
things would you write back home?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. We couldn't -- see, well, of course, they told us that it
was censored and to be careful not to give away locations
and things like that, but we could write pretty much "I'm
set on" -- you know, "I'm sitting here in this fox hole
and the snow all around, and -- but we haven't seen the Jerries," and, et cetera, you know. So it seemed like we
could write pretty much -- of course, you don't tell them
the bad stuff and tell them that things are pretty calm
and we're okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Remember anything about getting mail from home or
packages or anything?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Oh, yeah. I had a lot of correspondence from my parents
and my brothers and sisters and other relatives and
friends so I did pretty good on mail call which was
always a big event, you know when the mail would catch up
to us, which a lot of times was delayed, but, yeah, I did
good on letters and packages and cookies and this and
that. That was always a highlight, you know. They got
through pretty well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. What did you think of the Army food when you were out
there in the field?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, we were mostly on K-rations because we could pack
those away. They were just a little bit bigger than a
box of Cracker Jack, you know. It wasn't very good. It
was like cheese and -- cold cheese and what have you, but
whenever possible they would get the kitchens up there
and get us back for some hot food. It wasn't the
greatest, but it was hot so -- and they would get some
better rations as things calmed down a little. So we
always had enough, but it wasn't the greatest. That's for sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Do you remember hearing the news that FDR had died?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah, and that would have been about the time that we
were guarding those bridges in Germany there between the
Rhine and the Elbe. So that was -- yeah, that was kind
of a sad experience because most everybody liked FDR.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Was there a lot of sadness in the outfit though?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Oh, I don't know. I don't think that you notice it
particularly, but ...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. You seen so much of that anyways?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. Oh, yeah. Yeah. It was just another event.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. You obviously were in Germany then when they dropped the
bombs. Do you remember hearing the news about that and
trying to figure that out?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, yeah. I just -- just remember hearing the news
and, of course, we were just elated that it was all over,
and that we would -- you know, a lot of the guys would be
going home then to stay, and we just had nothing to worry
about as far as getting sent over to Japan which would --
we figured would be sort of a death knell for a lot of
the guys that had managed to get through the war over
there in Europe.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Do you remember doing anything to celebrate when the war
finally ended?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. No, because we was -- well, we -- well, we probably had some beer and wine and things like that but nothing big.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. VJ day came and it was just another day, right?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, it was just -- well, it was a great day for the
fact that it was over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. But we didn't have the facilities or the situation
probably to really celebrate like they did in a lot of --
Times Square or what have you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. When you finally got home, do you have memories of your
homecoming?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah. There was -- it wasn't until June of '46, first of
June, and I left from Bemmerhaben (ph) in Germany and had
a slow ride on a victory ship again in a rough -- rough
seas, which -- you know. Then we arrived in New York.
There was a smattering of people on the dock, the Red
Cross maybe and a few people to greet us, you know,
but -- maybe a dozen people or so and -- that wasn't a
big concern anyhow. The main thing was to see the Statue
of Liberty again for -- after a year and a half, and
then -- well, see, then we had a break and went back to
New York City and took a little tour there and then got
on the troop trains and went back up to Michigan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. What was it like to see your family again finally?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Oh, it was wonderful, you know, because I hadn't seen
them, you know, in a year and a half so that was a long time away so it was terrific to see them all again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Did they have a nice party for you?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. Well, if they did, I don't recall it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Well, it must have been a great party then.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. Yeah, right. I fell asleep. I don't recall.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Back to the other side of the ocean again, what -- did
you and your buddies do anything for entertainment,
anything to relieve the tension over there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. We had -- whenever there was a chance the USO was there
and the Red Cross was there with their doughnut wagons,
you know, and the gals. I remember a lot of the
dignitaries Bobby Bareen (ph) which he's an old timer, a
singer, and Mickey Rooney was there, and I'm not sure if
we saw Bob Hope or not. Probably did, but they would
come right up near the front and put on a show in the
barn and so that was always impressive when you get
something like that in the middle of everything, you
know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. And that was when the war was still going on?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And then more so after the war. Yeah,
those guys were over there right -- right when it was
happening. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. When you think about that experience overseas, does any
particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Not any one thing particularly. I would say that -- just the fact that we were put into -- thrust into it so fast,
you know, and so it was scary. Plus we were petrified
all the time, but -- when the war was going on. We just
sort of learned to live with it and keep going.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Did you get along okay with your officers?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah. Yeah, the officers and their sergeants and
commission and so on. Yeah, I didn't have a lot of
contact with them but -- except the platoon sergeant and
so on, but -- one of the second lieutenants gave me a
hard time because he told me I was going to have to take
a .45 and go out on a night patrol just -- just kind of
kidding around and scared me half to death, but that
didn't materialize.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Okay. A .45 on night patrol?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Yeah, right there in the middle of everything, and we
were well schooled in the M-1 and we had fired the .45,
you know, in our training but wasn't particularly anxious
to do anything like that because a lot of those patrols
were really problems and suffered a lot of casualties.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Anything else come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. I guess -- I guess that's -- basically covers it.
Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. All right. You'll think of something a few days later so
give me a call.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Oh, yeah. It's just -- all and all it was a -- it was an interesting experience, you know, to live through all
that and not even get scathed, you know, in all the death
and destruction going on around, and so you feel
fortunate to have gone through it. You know, even though
it's only two years out of your life and it happens 60
years ago or whatever, it's still vivid in your memory as
you probably know from your father.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. One thing that comes back, too, was over there in Belgium
we went by Malmadee (sic), and this was just a few days
after the Malmadee massacre. So that was a pretty
astounding story, and that's when the guys decided that
we aren't -- we aren't taking any prisoners anymore
because they were massacring our prisoners so that one --
that one stands out too, going right down that road
probably where those guys were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Did you come across any Germans after that where you
didn't take prisoners?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. Well, I didn't. I never got in a situation where I did,
but I -- you know, I was aware of it, and I saw our guys,
you know, do that to some of the prisoners but not
myself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p:
Q. Yeah, I talked to one guy locally and he said that they
do that. They took 50 or 60 German prisoners shortly
after that and paid them back.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. These -- yeah, these guys -- some of these guys had been
in the war way back in North Africa and Europe, and
they'd been there for years, you know, and we had been
there for months.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p:
A. So they were really bitter and -- different story with
them, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. Do you think that's got it?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Lawrence
sp.p: A. All right. Yeah, I think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Q. All right.
